title: Aging, nonstandard work, and technology are changing who finances social protection and who is covered
source_unit: OECD, Financing of Social Protection, published 9 September 2026
geography: OECD and European Union countries, with comparative analysis of social-protection financing, aging, work forms, labor income, pensions, health, long-term care, and family benefits

denominator.unit: OECD and EU social-protection financing comparison frame

social_protection_spending.unit: percent of GDP accounted for by social-protection expenditure in the OECD and EU, approximately

oecd_pension_spending_change.unit: percentage-point projected increase in OECD pension spending as a share of GDP between 2023 and 2045

oecd_health_ltc_spending_change.unit: percentage-point projected increase in OECD health and long-term-care spending as a share of GDP between 2023 and 2045

spending_pressure_set.value: population ageing, structural change, technology-driven job reallocation, and fiscal constraints

observations.method: OECD comparative analysis of public and private social-protection expenditure, financing mixes, demographic projections, labor income, and policy scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: Projected spending changes are scenario-dependent and do not establish future benefit adequacy, service quality, tax incidence, or household access in any specific country.
observations.subgroup: Older people, workers, caregivers, families, people needing health and long-term care, taxpayers, employers, pension institutions, and public budgets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Healthy aging, higher employment, productivity growth, prevention, family support, and better care organization could change spending paths; higher spending can also reflect expanded protection rather than deterioration.

denominator.unit: OECD and EU public social-spending financing frame

social_security_contribution_share_2023.unit: percent of OECD social spending financed through social-security contributions in 2023

social_security_contribution_share_1995.unit: percent of OECD social spending financed through social-security contributions in 1995

eu_employer_contribution_share.unit: percent of EU social contributions paid by employers, more than half

employment_risk_financing.value: social-security contributions finance 63 percent of earnings-related old-age and unemployment benefits versus 23 percent of family benefits

observations.method: OECD comparison of social-security contributions, general revenues, employer and employee financing, and benefit categories over time.
observations.uncertainty: Financing shares do not measure the ultimate incidence of contributions, benefit adequacy, labor-market effects, or the political feasibility of shifting financing sources.
observations.subgroup: Employees, employers, self-employed workers, families, pensioners, unemployed people, taxpayers, and social-insurance institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Contribution-linked financing can strengthen insurance and accountability, while general revenue can better fund benefits not tied to employment and protect people with unstable careers.

observations.period: 2023-2060; self-employment, work hours, and the financing base

denominator.unit: EU and OECD labor-income and social-protection financing frame

eu_self_employment_share.unit: percent of EU employment accounted for by self-employed workers

eu_self_employed_contribution_share.unit: percent of EU social-protection contributions accounted for by self-employed workers

oecd_hours_worked_change.unit: percent projected decline in total hours worked across the OECD between 2024 and 2060 under the report's scenario

eu_hours_worked_change.unit: percent projected decline in total hours worked across the EU over the same scenario

coverage_mechanism.value: formal coverage gaps, low take-up of voluntary schemes, incomplete risk pooling, and weaker unemployment-benefit coverage among self-employed workers

observations.method: OECD comparison of employment status, contribution records, coverage gaps, voluntary schemes, demographic projections, and total-hours scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: The hours scenarios do not forecast individual retirement, care, income, or labor-supply decisions; coverage patterns vary by country and work form.
observations.subgroup: Self-employed and platform workers, part-time workers, employees, older people, caregivers, employers, and people with unstable work histories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Self-employment can provide autonomy and entry, while expanded coverage and contribution subsidies can improve protection; higher employment among under-represented groups could offset aggregate hours decline, though not everywhere.

observations.period: 2026; financing redesign, capital income, inheritance, and care services

denominator.unit: OECD policy-options and social-protection financing frame

private_social_spending_eu.unit: percent of GDP represented by private social spending in the EU in 2021, average

labor_income_tax_base.value: about half of tax revenue is raised from labor income

policy_options.value: general revenues, capital and inheritance taxation, property taxation, contribution subsidies, formalization, and expanded coverage for self-employed workers

care_endpoint.value: health, long-term care, child benefits, poverty prevention, and care-leave credits may require financing less dependent on employment

observations.method: OECD policy analysis of alternative social-protection financing bases, demographic change, labor and capital income, inheritance, property, informality, and care-related benefits.
observations.uncertainty: Policy options involve distributional, administrative, behavioral, and political tradeoffs; the report does not identify a universally optimal financing mix or realized reform effects.
observations.subgroup: Workers, caregivers, families, pensioners, self-employed people, firms, asset holders, local governments, and recipients of health, long-term-care, family, and anti-poverty services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broader financing bases can improve resilience but may create new compliance and fairness disputes; capital and property taxes also face valuation, mobility, and administration constraints.

boundary: This record adds an aging-and-work-to-social-protection-financing route linking care, pensions, health, long-term care, labor income, self-employment, technology, taxes, and public budgets. It is not respondent-level household data, an individual care or pension trajectory, a universal tax recommendation, or proof that any financing reform was implemented or improved access.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD Financing of Social Protection publication page and executive summary were reviewed; spending projections, contribution shares, self-employed coverage, total-hours scenarios, financing-base options, and care-related boundaries were cross-checked.
